sections.h2: What is a quitclaim deed in Texas, and where does it fit?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed is one of several deed types the county clerk records in Texas, alongside general warranty, special warranty, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds. The Texas Supreme Court's county clerk manual lists it by name among the instruments filed in the deed records, and it is filed in the county where the land sits.

That list is about the extent of what the official pages say about the form itself. No state agency page in this research explains how much protection a quitclaim gives a buyer, so treat anyone's promise about that as a question for a title company or a Texas real estate attorney. What the official sources do cover is how any deed gets signed, recorded and followed by later steps such as probate, tax and sale.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. A buyer's title company reads every deed in the chain. A quitclaim anywhere in that chain can prompt extra questions, so the sooner you know what is in your own chain of title, the fewer surprises appear after you sign a sale contract.

sections.h2: What does a Texas deed need before the county clerk will record it?
sections.html:
The deed must be signed by the grantor and either acknowledged before an officer who can take acknowledgments or sworn, or signed before two subscribing witnesses. The clerk manual cites Property Code 12.001(b) for this rule and names a notary, a county clerk, a district clerk or a county court judge as officers who can take an acknowledgment.

  • Signature by the person giving up the interest.
  • An acknowledgment or sworn statement, or two subscribing witnesses.
  • Filing with the clerk of the county where the real property is located.
  • The recording fees the clerk charges, listed below.

Recording is how the public record shows who holds an interest. A deed that stays in a drawer does not appear in the clerk's records, and a later buyer or lender searching those records will not see it.

sections.h2: How much does the county clerk charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
The 2023 edition of the county clerk manual prints a per-page fee of $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page, plus smaller add-ons. Each clerk's current schedule is the number to rely on, so call the clerk in your county before you file.

The manual also notes that a missing grantee mailing address can add a $25 charge. A commissioners court may direct the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs.

sections.h2: Can a quitclaim deed move a house out of an estate?
sections.html:
Usually the route out of an estate runs through the probate paperwork, and a quitclaim signed by one heir does not replace it. The Texas State Law Library's deed guide describes which papers go on record for inherited real estate, depending on how the owner left it.

  • A transfer on death deed needs an affidavit of death and a death certificate recorded.
  • An administered estate needs an executor's or administrator's deed.
  • A muniment of title needs the court order and the will.
  • Without any of those, an affidavit of heirship may be used.

The same guide says the county cannot add heirs to the old deed. If you inherited a house in Texas, the clerk where it sits can tell you what the records show, and the library's probate guides explain the court options. A sworn affidavit of heirship carries no court verification, and the library notes that no law forces third parties to accept it.

sections.h2: What about a transfer on death deed or a Lady Bird deed instead?
sections.html:
Both avoid probate for the house, which is the reason owners ask about them as an alternative to a quitclaim to a relative. The State Law Library says a transfer on death deed passes real property without probate, can name charities as beneficiaries, can be cancelled by the owner, and must be recorded before the owner's death in the county where the property sits.

The library also describes the Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate deed, as one that lets the owner sell or mortgage without the beneficiary's consent. It adds that no official form exists. Because these deeds shape what a buyer can purchase later, a title company usually wants to see them before closing.

sections.h2: How do taxes and liens travel with a deed you sign?
sections.html:
A tax lien attaches on January 1 each year to secure that year's property taxes, and the Comptroller says the lien lets a court foreclose and seize the property even after ownership changes. The person who owned the property on January 1 stays liable for that year's tax and can be sued even after a sale.

Texas taxes are normally due by January 31, and unpaid bills turn delinquent on February 1 with a six percent penalty and one percent interest added. The Comptroller page notes that a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid. Giving the house away by quitclaim does not wipe out that lien, so ask the tax office in your county for the status of every year before you list or transfer.

sections.h2: What should I do before selling a house I hold by quitclaim?
sections.html:
Order a title search or call a title company early, and read each deed in your chain of title. Quitclaims, handwritten deeds, missing signatures and unrecorded transfers are the items that slow a closing.

  • Pull the recorded deeds from the county clerk and check each one for a signature and an acknowledgment.
  • Check whether every co-owner or heir signed.
  • Ask the county tax office for tax status for all years.
  • Ask the title company what it needs to insure a buyer.

If the chain has gaps that the title company cannot clear, a Texas real estate attorney can say whether a corrective instrument or a court action is the right fix. Cash buyers who purchase as-is will often still require a clean enough record for a title company to close, so the same review applies.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed recorded with the county clerk in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. The county clerk manual lists quitclaim deeds among the instruments filed in the deed records, in the county where the real property sits, after the deed is signed and acknowledged or witnessed.

faqs.q: What does recording a Texas deed cost?
faqs.a: The 2023 clerk manual prints $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, plus records fees of up to $10 twice and $2.00 for technology. Call your county clerk for the current schedule.

faqs.q: Can a quitclaim deed stop probate?
faqs.a: No source reviewed says it can. The State Law Library lists transfer on death deeds, muniments of title, administered-estate deeds and affidavits of heirship as the routes for inherited real property, so ask the clerk or a probate attorney before relying on a quitclaim.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim clear unpaid property taxes?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller says the January 1 tax lien lets a court foreclose even after ownership changes, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid.

faqs.q: Who can answer whether my quitclaim will pass title insurance?
faqs.a: A title company or a Texas real estate attorney. The official pages do not state how title insurers treat quitclaims, so the underwriter's own requirements control.
